When turning off the screen starts a meltdown

By CJ LimAutism Educator & Founder of APC

Reviewed 17 September 2026

You give a warning, the timer rings and the screen still does not go off easily. A difficult ending can involve leaving an enjoyable activity, an interruption at the wrong point or worry about what comes next. The same response will not fit every child or every screen activity.

In this guide
  • Understand what the screen is doing
  • Plan the ending before the difficult moment
  • Try, notice and adjust
  • When to seek more support

Understand what the screen is doing

A device may provide play, friendships, relaxation, learning or communication. Look at the activity and the transition, not only the minutes used. A warning helps some children; for others, repeated countdowns add stress. Observe your child's response rather than assuming either approach must work.

A communication device is not a reward. Keep access to AAC and other essential communication supports when setting limits on entertainment.

Plan the ending before the difficult moment

1

Agree a clear, practical endpoint

Use language or visuals your child understands: “One episode, then dinner.” Check the length, whether a game can be saved and whether the stopping point is realistic. Involve your child in planning where possible.

2

Choose a cue that fits

Try a visual timer, a single reminder or a natural stopping point. If a countdown increases distress, review it rather than making the countdown louder. Prepare for changes, such as an unexpected interruption or a video that runs longer than expected.

3

Make the next activity understandable

Say or show what comes next and have it ready. Check whether that activity is difficult in its own right. “Tablet away, then a snack together” is more concrete than “find something else to do”.

4

Support the transition and review it

Help save progress or finish the agreed step where appropriate. Keep your response calm. If distress escalates, prioritise safety and reduce extra demands. Review the plan later instead of assuming a harder reaction means you should enforce it more strictly.

If one device serves several purposes

Separate the entertainment activity from communication access where possible, for example by closing a game while leaving the communication app available. Ask the professionals supporting your child's AAC about practical setup. Do not remove their way to say “help”, “stop” or explain a problem.

Try, notice and adjust

Choose one regular screen transition. Record the activity, endpoint, cue, next activity and your child's response. Change one element that seems relevant. Look for a more understandable and manageable transition, not a promise of smaller meltdowns within a set number of weeks.

When to seek more support

If screen use or its endings repeatedly disrupt sleep, eating, school participation or family safety, discuss the pattern with an appropriate professional. Review other unmet needs and the wider routine alongside device boundaries.

Sources and further reading

  • NICE: supporting autistic children and young people
  • ASHA public guidance: augmentative and alternative communication

These sources inform the general guidance. The everyday examples are suggestions to adapt to your child, not an individual assessment or treatment plan.
